# Simulation results {#sec-sim}

We present the results in the order of the argument: the baseline fails on
the cutoff-based measures (@sec-sim-baseline), every remedy fixes sensitivity
(@sec-sim-sens), but for logistic regression none improves the ranking
(@sec-sim-rank), and resampling and weights distort the probabilities while
the threshold does not (@sec-sim-calib). The full table of changes with their
MCSEs is in Appendix @sec-app-tables.

## The baseline: accurate and nearly useless {#sec-sim-baseline}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-baseline
#| tbl-cap: "Baseline models (0.5 cutoff), averaged over both sample sizes and separations (400 replicates per cell)."
bl <- sim[sim$approach == "baseline", ]
t1 <- aggregate(cbind(accuracy, sensitivity, roc.auc, pr.auc) ~ classifier + prev, bl, mean)
t1 <- t1[order(t1$classifier, -t1$prev), ]
t1$classifier <- ifelse(t1$classifier == "logistic", "Lasso logistic", "Random forest")
t1$prev <- pct(t1$prev)
t1[, 3:6] <- lapply(t1[, 3:6], f3)
names(t1) <- c("Classifier", "Prevalence", "Accuracy", "Sensitivity", "ROC-AUC", "PR-AUC")
kable(t1, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE, align = "llrrrr")
```

@tbl-baseline shows the problem the remedies are meant to solve. At 1%
prevalence both baseline models are 99% accurate, but the lasso catches only
about 4% of positives and the forest about 2%. Accuracy is almost exactly
$1 - \pi$, what the "always negative" rule would score. Yet the ROC-AUCs
show the models *can* rank: the lasso's 0.80 is far above the 0.5 of a coin
flip. The models know which cases look risky; the 0.5 cutoff simply puts
almost all of them below the line. This is the first hint that the problem is
the cutoff, not the model.

## Every remedy raises sensitivity {#sec-sim-sens}

@fig-sens shows the change in sensitivity from the baseline, paired on the
same data sets. For the lasso every remedy raises sensitivity by about 0.6 to
0.7 at 1% and 5% prevalence, and by about 0.44 at 20%. For the forest,
under-sampling and the threshold give similar gains; SMOTE gives about a
third as much, over-sampling very little, and class weights actually *lower*
sensitivity slightly. At 50% prevalence nothing changes, as it should: the
data are already balanced.

![Change in sensitivity from the baseline (same data sets), pooled over the two separation levels: 200 replicates per point. Bars are $\pm 2$ MCSE, mostly smaller than the points.](figures/fig3_change_sensitivity.png){#fig-sens width=85%}

Judged by sensitivity, the remedies "work", and this is the evidence usually
given for them. The rest of this section asks whether anything else improved.

## For logistic regression, the ranking does not move {#sec-sim-rank}

@fig-roc shows the change in ROC-AUC. For the lasso the changes are
essentially zero: at $n = 20{,}000$ every remedy is within 0.005 of the
baseline in every one of the eight settings (Appendix @tbl-app-change). This is what the
intercept-only argument in @sec-remedies predicts. When the logistic model is
correct, resampling and weighting shift every log-odds by the same constant,
which cannot change the ranking.

![Change in ROC-AUC from the baseline (same data sets), 200 replicates per point, bars $\pm 2$ MCSE. For the lasso, every remedy sits on zero except at $n = 1{,}000$ and 1% prevalence.](figures/fig2_change_roc_auc.png){#fig-roc width=85%}

The one place the lasso moves is the hardest setting, $n = 1{,}000$ and 1%
prevalence, where a training set has about 10 positives. There,
under-sampling *lowers* ROC-AUC by 0.056 (MCSE 0.006), because the balanced
training set has only about 20 rows. Over-sampling and SMOTE *raise* it, by
0.014 and 0.016 (MCSE 0.004). The reason is a failure of the baseline rather
than a strength of resampling: with so few positives, cross-validation
sometimes chooses a $\lambda$ large enough to set every slope to zero, giving
the same prediction for every case and an ROC-AUC of exactly 0.5. This
happened in 25 of the 100 low-separation replicates for the baseline, never
after over-sampling or SMOTE, and in 42 after under-sampling. So with very
few positives, over-sampling can protect the lasso from shrinking to nothing.
Once there are enough positives ($n = 20{,}000$), the effect disappears.

**Forests are different.** For the random forest, under-sampling raises
ROC-AUC by 0.048 at 1% prevalence ($n = 1{,}000$) and 0.049
($n = 20{,}000$), both with MCSE of 0.003 or less, and by about 0.014 at 5%.
SMOTE helps at 1% (+0.022 and +0.016). Class weights *lower* ROC-AUC by up to
0.019. A forest has no intercept that resampling could shift, so resampling
changes the trees themselves. Our explanation for the gain is the forest's
coarse probabilities. With 1% positives, most leaves of a fully grown tree
contain no positives, so many test cases receive zero votes from every tree
and are tied at a predicted probability of 0. In the first replicate at 1%
prevalence ($n = 1{,}000$, high separation), 64% of the 20,000 test cases
had a predicted probability of exactly 0 from the baseline forest, and only
0.5% after under-sampling. Ties cannot be ranked, which lowers ROC-AUC.
Under-sampling gives every tree as many positives as negatives, so nearly
every case gets some votes and the ties break.
The weak effect of `classwt` is a known property of `randomForest()`: it
weights the split criterion but does not change which rows each tree sees.

@fig-gap uses PR-AUC, the measure that focuses on the rare class, and shows
each method's gap to the Bayes benchmark. Lower is better, and zero would mean
as good as the true probabilities.

![PR-AUC gap to the Bayes benchmark (true probabilities minus method), 200 replicates per point, bars $\pm 2$ MCSE. No remedy brings either classifier closer to the best possible than the baseline; for the forest, resampling and weights move it further away.](figures/fig4_gap_pr_auc.png){#fig-gap width=85%}

For the lasso at $n = 20{,}000$ every method is within 0.01 of the best
possible PR-AUC, and the remedies do not close the small remaining gap. For
the forest, *every* resampling remedy makes the gap larger. At 1%
prevalence and $n = 20{,}000$ the forest loses 0.050 PR-AUC with
over-sampling, 0.084 with SMOTE and 0.055 with under-sampling (all MCSE 0.003
or less). This includes under-sampling, which *raised* the forest's ROC-AUC.
The two measures disagree because they look at different parts of the
ranking. ROC-AUC counts every positive–negative pair, so breaking the mass of
ties at zero helps it. PR-AUC is driven by the top of the ranking, where the
alarms are raised. A forest trained on 50:50 data gives high probabilities to
many more negatives, so the top of the ranking contains more false alarms and
precision falls.

## The threshold gives the same gains and honest probabilities {#sec-sim-calib}

If the remedies do not improve the ranking, what do they change? They change
the predicted probabilities. A model is *calibrated* if, among cases given a
probability of about 5%, about 5% are positive. A simple check is
"calibration in the large": the average predicted probability on the test
set should equal the prevalence. We refitted the remedies on 5 replicates per
setting ($n = 20{,}000$, high separation), using the same seeds, so the fits
are identical to those in the main study (the ROC-AUCs match exactly), and
recorded the mean predicted probability and the Brier score, the mean of
$(\hat p - y)^2$ (lower is better).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-calib
#| tbl-cap: "Calibration in the large: mean predicted probability and Brier score on the test set (n = 20,000, high separation, 5 replicates per setting). The threshold approach uses the baseline model, so it has the baseline's probabilities. Source: analysis/11_calibration.R."
cal <- read.csv("results/table_calibration.csv")
cal$approach <- factor(cal$approach,
                       levels = c("baseline", "oversample", "undersample", "smote", "weights"),
                       labels = c("Baseline / threshold", "Over-sampling", "Under-sampling",
                                  "SMOTE", "Class weights"))
cal$cell <- sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", cal$mean.prob, cal$brier)
cal$prev.lab <- pct(cal$prev)
cw <- reshape(cal[, c("classifier", "approach", "prev.lab", "cell")],
              idvar = c("classifier", "approach"), timevar = "prev.lab", direction = "wide")
names(cw) <- sub("cell.", "", names(cw))
cw <- cw[order(cw$classifier != "logistic", cw$approach), c("classifier", "approach", "1%", "5%", "20%")]
cw$classifier <- ifelse(cw$classifier == "logistic", "Lasso logistic", "Random forest")
names(cw)[1:2] <- c("Classifier", "Approach")
kable(cw, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE, align = "llrrr")
```

@tbl-calib gives the mean predicted probability, with the Brier score in
brackets. The baseline lasso is well calibrated: at 1% prevalence its average
prediction is 0.010. Every remedy raises the average to about 0.2 at 1%
prevalence, 0.25 at 5% and 0.36 at 20%. At 1% the model now "believes"
positives are about 20 times more common than they are, and its Brier score
is about 12 times worse (0.10 against 0.009). For the forest, under-sampling has the same effect (0.25 at 1%)
and SMOTE a smaller one; over-sampling and class weights change the forest's
probabilities little, which matches their small effect on sensitivity in
@fig-sens.

The threshold approach reaches the same sensitivity without this cost.
@tbl-example compares the baseline, over-sampling and the threshold for the
lasso at 5% prevalence and $n = 20{,}000$.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-example
#| tbl-cap: "Lasso logistic regression at 5% prevalence, n = 20,000, high separation: mean over 100 replicates (mean predicted probability: 5 replicates, from the calibration table above)."
ex <- sim[sim$classifier == "logistic" & sim$prev == 0.05 & sim$n == 20000 &
          sim$sep.level == "high" & sim$approach %in% c("baseline", "oversample", "threshold"), ]
te <- aggregate(cbind(cutoff, sensitivity, specificity, roc.auc, pr.auc) ~ approach, ex, mean)
mp <- cal$mean.prob[cal$classifier == "logistic" & cal$prev == 0.05]
names(mp) <- c("baseline", "oversample", "undersample", "smote", "weights")[match(
  as.character(cal$approach[cal$classifier == "logistic" & cal$prev == 0.05]),
  c("Baseline / threshold", "Over-sampling", "Under-sampling", "SMOTE", "Class weights"))]
te$mean.prob <- c(baseline = mp[["baseline"]], oversample = mp[["oversample"]],
                  threshold = mp[["baseline"]])[te$approach]
te$approach <- c(baseline = "Baseline", oversample = "Over-sampling",
                 threshold = "Threshold (baseline model)")[te$approach]
te[, 2:7] <- lapply(te[, 2:7], f3)
names(te) <- c("Approach", "Cutoff", "Sensitivity", "Specificity", "ROC-AUC", "PR-AUC",
               "Mean predicted P")
kable(te, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrrr")
```

Over-sampling and the threshold reach nearly the same sensitivity and
specificity, with identical ranking. The difference is *how*. Over-sampling
refits the model on altered data and inflates every probability, so the cutoff
of 0.5 now sits where the true probability is about 0.05. The threshold keeps
the honest model and moves the cutoff to about 0.05 directly. The two routes
lead to the same decisions, but only the threshold leaves probabilities
that can still be read as probabilities, which matters whenever the number
itself is used: to set a price, to rank cases by urgency, or to explain a
decision. The threshold also needs no refitting and states the cost
trade-off openly: a cutoff of 0.05 says a missed positive is treated as
$(1 - 0.05)/0.05 = 19$ times as costly as a false alarm. This agrees with
@vandengoorbergh2022, who reached the same conclusion for logistic risk
models in medicine.

## What the simulation shows

Taken together, the simulation gives a clear picture. Every remedy raises
sensitivity, often from below 0.1 to about 0.7, which is why they look
successful when sensitivity is the measure. For the correctly specified lasso,
however, none of them improves ROC-AUC or PR-AUC once there are enough
positives to learn from. The only exception is the setting with about 10
positives, where over-sampling and SMOTE help by stopping the lasso from
shrinking to a model with no slopes, and under-sampling makes things worse.
What resampling and weights do change is the probabilities, which they
inflate about 20-fold at 1% prevalence and 5-fold at 5%. Moving the threshold
reaches the same sensitivity and keeps the probabilities calibrated.

The forest tells a different story. Under-sampling and SMOTE raise its
ROC-AUC at 1% prevalence, but every resampling method lowers its PR-AUC, and
class weights hurt both. Finally, sample size matters at least as much as
balance. Going from $n = 1{,}000$ to $n = 20{,}000$ at 1% prevalence raises
the baseline ROC-AUC by about 0.05 for both classifiers, as much as the best
remedy, and it raises PR-AUC, which no remedy does.
